# What Does 50% Aromatic Content Mean for Petroleum Tank Truck Hose Selection?
## What Does "Aromatic Content" Mean in Fuel Transfer?
Historical shifts in fuel refinement forced manufacturers to innovate rapidly. Removing lead and increasing octane via aromatics required entirely new polymer formulations. Legacy rubber degraded within weeks when exposed to modern unleaded gasoline. The fluid transfer industry established the 50% aromatic threshold as the absolute baseline requirement. This standard ensures equipment can handle the baseline solvency of modern fuel blends without immediate structural failure.
## Evaluating Tube Materials for Chemical Compatibility
Evaluating **oil tank truck hose chemical compatibility** requires a deep understanding of polymer capabilities. Commodity Nitrile (NBR) often handles 30% or lower aromatics. It fails quickly in modern, high-octane fuel applications. Specially compounded high-grade NBR tubes withstand up to 50% aromatics safely. Premium variations now achieve a 55% rating.
Extreme applications demand advanced, high-performance polymers. Highly aromatic crude, aromatic-based solvents, or heavily additized fuels easily exceed standard NBR limits. FKM (fluoroelastomer), specialized polyurethane, or ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene (UHMWPE) provide the necessary resistance. These advanced materials handle aggressive chemical attacks without swelling or softening. They maintain their structural integrity even under continuous exposure to pure BTX compounds.

ceramic.snippet:
Last year, Honda proudly launched its new hydrogen powered fuel cell car - the FCX - which boasts a maximum speed of 93 mph and ’zero emissions’.

  If one conservatively assumes that a vehicle’s physical system - everything needed to deliver hydrogen to the fuel cell: tanks, heaters, chillers, pumps, tubes and hoses - weighs about one third to half the weight of the storage material then the target material should approach a minimum of 12 weight per cent of hydrogen. This implies that the elements that make up materials for on-board hydrogen storage can only come from the first two rows of the periodic table. However, small amounts of higher weight elements could be tolerated at low concentrations for catalytic purposes. 

  Ammonia is another potential chemical storage medium and has the advantage, in comparison with hydrocarbons, that the thermodynamics of hydrogen release are more favourable - less endothermic - and there is no onboard CO 2  emission. However, ammonia is toxic both to people and to polymer electrolyte membrane (PEM) fuel cells and various approaches have been proposed to lower its volatility. For example, Jens N?rskov and his team at the Technical University of Denmark have recently shown that ammonia can be stored as a solid in a metal ammine complex. 

  The Pacific Northwest team, part of the DOE Center of excellence in chemical hydrogen storage, has developed a way to deposit ammonia borane within the porous channels of mesoporous silica. The silica increases the rate of hydrogen release from the ammonia borane by two orders of magnitude compared with the release of hydrogen from ammonia borane alone. Furthermore, heating the hybrid material above 370K to release the second equivalent of hydrogen gives rise to very little borazine, a volatile impurity that needs to be minimised to avoid poisoning PEM fuel cells.

claude-search.snippet: Recent environmental regulations imposed on the automotive industry and on the fuel delivery industries severely limit the amount of fuel vapor that can permeate from the fuel system of motor vehicles and from the fuel delivery hoses used to transport such fuels. Typically, fuel transfer hoses, in the past, have been constructed of natural or synthetic rubber material such as butadiene-acrylonitrile rubber or the like. Other hoses have been constructed using a fluoroelastomer as an inner wall surface layer of the hose and some other material as the outer layer. Such hoses have a high permeability to fuel vapor. Attempts to produce fuel transport hoses with reduced permeability to fuel vapors have included the use of corrugated polyamide and fluorocarbon thermoplastic tubes. For example, such hoses are discussed in U.S. Polybutylene terephthalate has been used as a thin barrier layer in multilayer hoses or tubes as disclosed in U.S. Other examples of prior art patents which teach multilayer polymer hoses or tubes containing polybutylene terephthalate in one of the layers include U.S. which teaches a multi-layer assembly for use in fuel line applications, wherein the multiphase polymer may be polybutylene terephthalate and U.S. which teaches rubber hoses composed of an inner tube of polybutylene terephthalate. ## What Is NBR Rubber?

NBR is a family of unsaturated copolymers made from butadiene and acrylonitrile (ACN). The polar nitrile groups are a major reason NBR performs well with many petroleum oils, lubricants and greases, while the butadiene portion contributes elastomeric flexibility. NBR is also widely known as nitrile rubber or Buna-N.

“NBR” is not a complete material specification. The polymer grade, ACN level, molecular structure, fillers, plasticizers, antioxidants, cure package and processing history all influence the finished compound. Two parts labeled “NBR 70 Shore A” can therefore show different oil swell, low-temperature behavior, compression set, abrasion resistance and aging performance.

linkup.snippet:
A flexible hose having a non-fluorinated rubber inner tube, a non-fluorinated rubber outer cover, an intermediate barrier layer consisting essentially of ethylene-vinyl alcohol copolymer (EVOH) having an ethylene content less than 30 mole %, and preferably a textile reinforcement between said barrier layer and said outer cover.
High crystallinity makes EVOH a brittle, rigid polymer with poor low-temperature flexibility. Thus, typical hose designs have required 30 to 50 mole % ethylene content for satisfactory flexibility. Alternately, or in addition, typical designs have used very thin EVOH layers coupled with additional layers of other barrier materials such as fluoropolymers, polyolefins, and/or polyamides. SUMMARY · The present invention is directed to systems and methods which provide a low-permeation fuel hose suitable for example for use with alcohol-containing fuels and which is very flexible.
Specifically the present invention provides a very low permeation rubber fuel hose based on non-fluorinated elastomer with an intermediate EVOH barrier layer of very low-ethylene EVOH, optionally reinforced with nylon textile. Nylon 12 fuel line material has emerged as a critical engineering thermoplastic in automotive fuel delivery systems, offering an exceptional balance of chemical resistance, mechanical durability, and permeation barrier performance. This polyamide-12 polymer, synthesized from laurolactam monomer, exhibits superior resistance to hydrocarbons, alcohols, and aggressive fuel additives while maintaining flexibility across wide temperature ranges (-40°C to +150°C).
Nylon 12 fuel line material derives its performance characteristics from the polyamide-12 backbone structure, featuring twelve carbon atoms between amide linkages (-CO-NH-). This extended aliphatic chain length compared to Nylon 6 (six carbons) or Nylon 6,6 (average six carbons) results in reduced amide group density, conferring lower moisture sensitivity and enhanced chemical resistance 1. The polymer exhibits a semi-crystalline morphology with typical crystallinity ranging from 35% to 45%, melting point of approximately 178°C, and glass transition temperature near 40-50°C 6.
Multi-layer fuel line constructions integrate high-barrier polymers to meet increasingly stringent evaporative emission standards (CARB LEV III: <15 mg/m·day permeation at 40°C) 2. Polyethylene terephthalate (PET) films (trade name MYLAR) at 25-50 μm thickness provide hydrocarbon permeation reduction factors of 8-12× compared to Nylon 12 alone 2.
For multi-layer coextrusion, a feedblock or multi-manifold die system combines melt streams from separate extruders, with layer thickness control achieved through individual extruder speed adjustment and rheological matching of polymer melts 2.

seltz.title: How To Clean Buying: A Materials Scientist’s Practical Framework for Sustainable, High-Performance Material Procurement
seltz.snippet:
"How to clean buying" is not about aesthetics—it’s a precision-driven procurement discipline rooted in materials science. It means systematically eliminating chemical impurities, particulate residues, moisture, extractables, and undocumented additives that compromise performance, regulatory compliance, or longevity. For example, medical-grade silicone tubing from NuSil must contain <10 ppm residual platinum catalyst; automotive polyamide 66 (e.g., BASF Ultramid B3WG6) requires ≤50 ppm chloride ions to prevent corrosion in EV battery housings; and semiconductor-grade copper foil (supplied by Furukawa Electric) demands oxygen content <5 ppm and surface roughness Ra <0.2 µm. This article details the five-stage framework used by Tier-1 aerospace suppliers and FDA-audited device manufacturers: specification anchoring, supplier qualification, lot-level analytical verification, functional validation, and lifecycle traceability. We cite 17 ASTM/ISO standards, reference 9 real material systems, and provide actionable thresholds—not theoretical ideals.

## Why "Clean" Is a Quantifiable, Not Qualitative, Attribute

In materials engineering, "clean" is rigorously defined—not inferred. ASTM E2412-22 defines cleanliness for optical polymers as ≤0.5 particles/mm² larger than 5 µm under controlled white-light microscopy. ISO 16232-10:2022 sets particle-count limits for fuel injection components: Class 5 allows only 30 particles ≥15 µm per 100 mL of extraction fluid. These aren’t marketing claims—they’re enforceable pass/fail criteria. When Boeing procures titanium alloy Ti-6Al-4V (AMS 4911), it mandates ≤25 ppm total metallic contaminants (Fe, Ni, Cu) and ≤10 ppm oxygen—verified via glow discharge mass spectrometry (GDMS). ## Materials Used to Make a 5/16 Braided Fuel Hose

A **5/16 braided fuel hose** is a critical component in fuel delivery systems, especially in automotive, marine, and performance applications. Designed to handle pressurized fuel under extreme conditions, these hoses are constructed from multiple layers of specialized materials. Each layer serves a distinct purpose—ensuring durability, chemical resistance, pressure tolerance, and longevity. Below is a detailed breakdown of the key materials used in their construction.

#### Nitrile Rubber (NBR)

Also known as acrylonitrile-butadiene rubber (ANR), nitrile is the most common inner tube material in fuel hoses due to its exceptional resistance to hydrocarbons.

##### Advantages

- High resistance to gasoline, diesel, and oil
- Maintains flexibility across a wide temperature range (-40°F to +250°F)
- Durable under prolonged fuel exposure
- Prevents fuel permeation and degradation

##### Limitations

- Limited compatibility with high-ethanol biofuels (E85+)
- Less resistant to ozone and UV radiation
- May degrade faster in outdoor environments

Best for: Standard gasoline engines, carbureted systems, classic cars

#### Reinforcing Braids (Polyester & Aramid)

The middle layer consists of tightly woven synthetic fibers—typically polyester or aramid (e.g., Kevlar®)—that provide structural strength and pressure resistance.

##### Advantages

- High tensile strength prevents bursting
- Resists kinking and collapsing under vacuum
- Supports operating pressures up to 300+ PSI
- Enhances overall hose durability and safety

##### Limitations

- Aramid is more expensive than polyester
- Braiding quality affects performance consistency
- Damage during installation can compromise integrity

Best for: High-performance engines, forced induction systems, racing applications

Official approval already exists to continue raising the proportion to 10% – the E10 level, and quite simply, none of this is good news for classic vehicle owners, for old car fuel systems and Ethanol were never intended to meet.

Ethanol is not a pleasant substance, being acidic, somewhat corrosive, a solvent, and also hygroscopic – it absorbs water from the atmosphere. Over time, water and ethanol form a mix denser than petrol, and in a process known technically as “phase separation” this pretty aggressive cocktail sinks to the bottom of the tank. With E10, the process starts with a mere 0.5% water content in the fuel.

In modern and well-used vehicles running on E5 fuel, neither the amount of water build-up nor phase separation has proven to be a big worry, since with occasional exceptions, cars of the 21st century can accommodate it.
